name: Makara Saṅkrānti
summary: The Sun's entry into sidereal Capricorn (Makara), the year's principal solar festival and the traditional start of Uttarāyaṇa.
note: Sidereal (nirāyana) anchor: solar longitude 270° measured from a fixed origin, NOT the tropical winter solstice. Precession has separated the two by roughly 24° since they last coincided around 291 CE, which is why the festival now falls 14–15 January rather than ~21–22 December; the Gregorian date drifts about one day per 70–72 years. Implementations must apply an ayanāṃśa — the Indian civil ephemeris uses Chitrāpakṣa (Lahiri), defined against a fixed point opposite Spica/Citrā — and the Raman and Krishnamurti ayanāṃśas differ by up to about a degree, which can move the computed moment across a day boundary. Separately, the day the festival is KEPT is not always the day of the astronomical saṅkrānti: when the saṅkrānti moment falls at night the nibandhas shift the puṇyakāla to an adjacent day, and Nirṇayasindhu and Dharmasindhu do not give identical cutoffs, so pañcāṅgas occasionally disagree by one day. Being solar, it does not move with the tithi and is wholly unaffected by adhika māsa. Regional forms: Pongal (Tamil Nadu, four days), Uttarāyaṇa (Gujarat), Māgha/Bhogāli Bihu (Assam), Māghī (Punjab), Poush Sankranti (Bengal), Khichdi (eastern UP/Bihar).

name: Vasant Pañcamī
summary: Fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, kept as the onset of spring and as the principal worship of Sarasvatī.
note: Māgha śukla pañcamī. Śukla-pakṣa, so amānta and pūrṇimānta name the same month — no reckoning ambiguity. Pūjā is performed in the pūrvāhṇa (the first part of the day), so the day kept is the one on which pañcamī is current during the forenoon. Yellow dress and offerings; children are traditionally given their first letters (akṣarābhyāsa / vidyārambha) on this day. The Sarasvatī identification dominates present practice — Sarasvatī Pūjā in Bengal, Odisha, Assam and Bihar — but it is not the only classical reading: the name Śrī Pañcamī, still standard in the south and in Odisha, reflects an older association with Śrī/Lakṣmī and with the season itself, and vrata literature treats the day under both headings. Do not assume the two names mark different days; they mark the same tithi. In Bali the same day is kept as Hari Raya Saraswati, but on the 210-day Pawukon cycle, so it is not calendrically commensurable with the Indian date.

name: Mahā Śivarātri
summary: The great night of Śiva, kept as a night-long vigil and fast on the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight preceding the spring new moon.
note:
RECKONING SPLIT — the same night, two month names. Amānta regions (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Goa, Karnataka, Andhra, Telangana, Tamil Nadu) call it Māgha kṛṣṇa caturdaśī; pūrṇimānta regions (most of North and Central India) call it Phālguna kṛṣṇa caturdaśī. There is no disagreement about the day. The anchor here is given amāntically; the pūrṇimānta name is recorded as a variant. Because this is a NIGHT observance, centred on niśīta kāla (the middle watch, roughly the eighth muhūrta, around solar midnight), the day kept is the one on whose night caturdaśī prevails at niśīta — not necessarily the day on which caturdaśī is current at sunrise. This is the single commonest source of one-day errors in Śivarātri software, and Śaiva and Smārta nirṇaya can diverge when caturdaśī straddles the midnight boundary. Worship proceeds in four prahara pūjās through the night; pāraṇa the next morning. Distinct from the Māsa Śivarātri of every month's kṛṣṇa caturdaśī — Mahā Śivarātri is specifically the Māgha/Phālguna one.

Day rule: niśītha — the great night of Śiva; the niśītha kāla worship is the defining rite.

name: Holikā Dahan
summary: The bonfire on the eve of Holi, burning the demoness Holikā and marking the victory of Prahlāda's devotion over Hiraṇyakaśipu.
note: Phālguna pūrṇimā — śukla 15. Being a pūrṇimā it is śukla pakṣa, so amānta and pūrṇimānta agree on the month name; note only that in pūrṇimānta reckoning this is the LAST day of Phālguna, while amāntically it is mid-month. The fire is kindled in pradoṣa kāla, after sunset. Two nirṇaya rules regularly move the observance off the naive 'evening of the full moon': (1) Bhadrā (the Viṣṭi karaṇa) is excluded, and if Bhadrā occupies the early night the dahan is deferred to after Bhadrā-mukha or to a later muhūrta, occasionally past midnight; (2) when pūrṇimā is current at sunset on two successive days, or on neither, the nibandhas apply priority rules that can shift the bonfire a day. Consequence for implementers: Holikā Dahan and Rangwāli Holi are NOT guaranteed to be consecutive Gregorian dates. Also Dol Pūrṇimā / Dol Jātrā in Bengal and Odisha and Śigmo in Goa and the Konkan fall on this pūrṇimā itself, i.e. the day BEFORE the North Indian colour play — a genuine regional difference of day, not of name.

name: Holi (Rangwāli Holi / Dhulaṇḍī)
summary: The day of coloured powder and water, kept on the first lunar day after the Phālguna full moon.
note: RECKONING SPLIT, and an unusually treacherous one. Amāntically this is Phālguna kṛṣṇa pratipadā; pūrṇimāntically it is CHAITRA kṛṣṇa pratipadā, because in pūrṇimānta reckoning the month turns at the full moon and the colour day opens Chaitra. So North Indian almanacs place Holi in Chaitra even though it is universally spoken of as the Phālguna festival — and a system that stores the popular month name 'Phālguna' and evaluates it pūrṇimāntically, or stores an almanac's 'Chaitra' and evaluates it amāntically, will be a month out. The anchor is amānta; the pūrṇimānta form is recorded as a variant. Regional names: Dhulaṇḍī, Dhuleṭi, Dhulivandan, Rangwāli Holi, Phagwā. The Braj cycle is much longer than one day, running from about Phālguna śukla 9 (Lāṭhmār Holi at Barsānā and Nandgaon) through Raṅgbharī Ekādaśī (śukla 11) to Huranga at Dāūjī on the day after Dhulaṇḍī. Bengal and Odisha keep Dol Jātrā on the preceding pūrṇimā instead, so 'Holi' there is a different Gregorian day. Not observed in an adhika Phālguna; the observance waits for nija Phālguna.

name: Vāsantika (Chaitra) Navarātri
summary: The spring nine nights of the Goddess, running from the first to the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra.
note: Chaitra śukla 1 through śukla 9. Śukla pakṣa, so both reckonings name the month Chaitra — no ambiguity. Opens with ghaṭasthāpanā / kalaśa-sthāpanā on pratipadā in a prescribed muhūrta and closes on Rāma Navamī; some lineages extend to śukla 10. The same pratipadā is the year-head in much of India: Gudi Padwa (Maharashtra), Ugādi (Karnataka, Andhra, Telangana), Saṃsāra Pāḍvo (Konkan), Navreh (Kashmir), and the Chaitrādi Vikrama Saṃvat new year of North and Central India; Cheti Chand (Sindhi) is kept on śukla 2. IMPLEMENTATION CAVEAT: the nine days are nine TITHIS, not nine solar days — a kṣaya-tithi compresses the run into eight Gregorian days and a vṛddhi-tithi stretches it to ten, so `days: 9` is nominal and a correct implementation should generate the span tithi-by-tithi rather than by adding eight days. Not observed in an adhika Chaitra; the festival waits for nija Chaitra. Distinct from the two Gupta Navarātris (Māgha śukla 1–9 and Āṣāḍha śukla 1–9), which are regionally and individually kept rather than pan-Indian and are not included in this corpus.

name: Rāma Navamī
summary: The birth of Rāma, kept at midday on the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra.
note:
Chaitra śukla navamī; both reckonings agree. Vālmīki places the birth in Caitra, on the navamī tithi, under 'the nakṣatra whose deity is Aditi' — that is Punarvasu — with Karka lagna and five planets in exaltation (Bālakāṇḍa 18.8–10); modern pañcāṅgas note the Punarvasu coincidence when it occurs but do not require it, and the tithi alone governs. TIMING RULE: the observance falls in madhyāhna, the middle third of the daylight period, so the day kept is the one on which navamī is current at midday. A navamī that begins only in the afternoon pushes the festival to the following day even though navamī is technically 'current' on the earlier date — a common off-by-one. Concludes Chaitra Navarātri. Kept as Sītā-Rāma Kalyāṇam in Telugu practice, most famously at Bhadrāchalam, where the celestial wedding rather than the birth is the focus.

Day rule: madhyāhna — Rāma is born at madhyāhna; the birth hour decides the day.

name: Akṣaya Tṛtīyā
summary: The 'undiminishing third', a day on which any meritorious act is held to yield inexhaustible fruit, on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
note: Vaiśākha śukla tṛtīyā; both reckonings agree. One of the sāḍhe-tīn muhūrta — the three and a half wholly auspicious days of the traditional year — and therefore held to need no separate muhūrta calculation for undertakings, which is the substance of the observance. Kept in the pūrvāhṇa. Merit is held to be heightened when the tithi coincides with Rohiṇī nakṣatra or falls on a Monday, but neither is required. Also Paraśurāma Jayantī; the tradition making it the start of Tretā Yuga and the day Vyāsa began dictating the Mahābhārata is Purāṇic and late. The Cār Dhām shrines at Badrīnāth, Kedārnāth, Gaṅgotrī and Yamunotrī open on or about this day, and Chandana Yātrā begins at Puri. In Jain reckoning it commemorates Ṛṣabhadeva breaking his year-long fast with sugarcane juice. CAVEAT: the modern mass purchase of gold on this day is a twentieth-century commercial development with no śāstric prescription behind it; entries that describe it as a traditional requirement are repeating advertising.

name: Guru Pūrṇimā (Vyāsa Pūrṇimā)
summary: The full moon of Āṣāḍha, kept in honour of the teacher and of Veda Vyāsa, and marking the opening of the rains retreat.
note: Āṣāḍha śukla 15. Pūrṇimā is śukla pakṣa, so amānta and pūrṇimānta name the same month; note only that pūrṇimāntically this is the last day of Āṣāḍha and amāntically its midpoint. Pūjā of one's guru and of Vyāsa, whose birth and whose division of the Vedas the day commemorates — hence Vyāsa Pūrṇimā. CAVEAT on Cāturmāsya: the four-month monastic retreat is commonly said to begin here, and for saṃnyāsins it does, but many Vaiṣṇava authorities reckon Cāturmāsya from Devaśayanī Ekādaśī (Āṣāḍha śukla 11) instead, and some from the Āṣāḍha saṅkrānti; the four months end at Kārtika Pūrṇimā or at Prabodhinī Ekādaśī correspondingly. Do not treat the retreat's start as settled. The same full moon is Āsāḷha Pūjā in Theravāda Buddhism, commemorating the first sermon at Sārnāth and opening vassa — a genuine shared date rather than a coincidence of naming, though the Buddhist calendar's own intercalation can separate the two by a lunation in some years.

name: Nāga Pañcamī
summary: Worship of the serpent deities on the fifth lunar day of Śrāvaṇa — bright fortnight in most of India, dark fortnight in several western and northern regions.
note: MARKED DISPUTED, and deliberately not resolved. The dominant and most widely almanacked date is Śrāvaṇa ŚUKLA pañcamī, which is the anchor given here; being śukla pakṣa, both reckonings name the month Śrāvaṇa. But several regions keep a KṚṢṆA-pakṣa pañcamī instead, and this is a difference of DAY, not merely of month name. Gujarat keeps Śrāvaṇ Vad Pāñcam — amānta Śrāvaṇa kṛṣṇa 5 — roughly a fortnight AFTER the śukla date. Standard references also report kṛṣṇa-pakṣa observance in Rajasthan and Bihar, described as 'the dark half of the same month'; but those states reckon pūrṇimānta, where 'Śrāvaṇa kṛṣṇa 5' denotes amānta Āṣāḍha kṛṣṇa 5, roughly ten days BEFORE the śukla date. The identical phrase therefore names two different days depending on the region's reckoning, and I could not verify which the Rajasthani and Bihari observances actually keep. An implementation must not silently normalise these to one date. Related but distinct observances that should not be merged: Garuḍa Pañcamī and Nāga Caturthī in parts of the Deccan and Andhra, and the Battis Shirala observance in Maharashtra, which follows the śukla date. Milk and lampblack offerings at anthills and serpent images; ploughing and digging are avoided.

name: Rakṣā Bandhan
summary: The full moon of Śrāvaṇa, on which a protective thread is tied — in modern northern practice by a sister on her brother's wrist.
note: Śrāvaṇa śukla 15; both reckonings agree. Kept in the aparāhṇa, and the standard nirṇaya excludes Bhadrā (the Viṣṭi karaṇa). Because Bhadrā very often occupies the opening stretch of the pūrṇimā, pañcāṅgas frequently publish a narrow afternoon or evening window rather than the whole day, and in some years the permitted window falls after sunset — implementations that assume 'all day' will be wrong about the muhūrta even when right about the date. The same full moon carries several distinct observances: Śrāvaṇī Upākarma, the annual renewal of the yajñopavīta (kept on this day by Ṛgvedins and Yajurvedins, while Sāmavedins keep Upākarma separately in Bhādrapada under Hasta nakṣatra); Narali Pūrṇimā on the Konkan coast; Jhulan Pūrṇimā in Bengal; Gamha Pūrṇimā in Odisha; Janai Pūrṇimā in Nepal. HISTORICAL CAVEAT: the day's older attested content is the Upākarma and the tying of a rakṣā or apotropaic thread generally; the brother–sister rite in its present form is comparatively recent and predominantly northern, and its diffusion southward and westward is a twentieth-century phenomenon. Do not read the modern form back into the Purāṇic citations.

name: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
summary: The midnight birth of Kṛṣṇa, on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight preceding the Bhādrapada new moon.
note:
RECKONING SPLIT plus a genuine sampradāya split — two separate problems, both of which must be modelled. (1) NAMING: amānta regions call the day Śrāvaṇa kṛṣṇa aṣṭamī; pūrṇimānta regions call the identical day Bhādrapada kṛṣṇa aṣṭamī. Same night. The anchor is amānta; the pūrṇimānta name is a variant. (2) DAY SELECTION: Smārta and Vaiṣṇava nirṇaya can genuinely land on different Gregorian dates. Smārta authorities take the aṣṭamī prevailing at niśītha (midnight), since the birth is placed at midnight; Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava and ISKCON practice requires aṣṭamī at sunrise and weights the conjunction with Rohiṇī nakṣatra more heavily. When aṣṭamī and Rohiṇī do not overlap cleanly the two traditions can be one day apart. This is not a rounding artefact and should not be collapsed. Kept as a day-long fast broken at midnight, or in some traditions at the end of the tithi or nakṣatra the following morning. In Maharashtra the popular observance is the following day's Dahi Handi / Gopālakāla (kṛṣṇa 9), so the 'festival' there is effectively two days.

Day rule: niśītha — Kṛṣṇa is born at midnight; the birth hour decides the day.

name: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
summary: The installation and worship of Gaṇeśa from the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, ending in immersion on Ananta Caturdaśī.
note:
Bhādrapada śukla caturthī; both reckonings agree. TIMING: the sthāpanā is kept in madhyāhna, so the day chosen is the one on which caturthī is current at MIDDAY, not at sunrise — a caturthī beginning in the afternoon defers the festival. DURATION: `days: 11` counts inclusively from śukla 4 to the public visarjana on Ananta Caturdaśī, śukla 14; the festival is nevertheless universally described as ten days, because ten nights intervene. Both figures are correct under different counting and neither is an error. Household observances commonly end after 1½, 3, 5, 7 or 11 days, so any given family's span is shorter than the public one. The chandra-darśana-niṣedha applies: seeing the moon on this night is held to bring the mithyā-doṣa, the false accusation, and the prescribed remedy is recitation of the Syamantaka episode. The mass sārvajanik form dates from Lokmanya Tilak's reorganisation of the festival at Pune in 1893 and is a documented modern innovation; the domestic vrata is far older and should not be dated from Tilak.

name: Śāradīya Navarātri
summary: The autumn nine nights of the Goddess, from the first to the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
note: Āśvina śukla 1 through śukla 9; both reckonings agree. Opens with ghaṭasthāpanā on pratipadā. REGIONAL STRUCTURE DIFFERS, and this is not merely nomenclature: in Bengal, Assam and Odisha the operative festival is Durgā Pūjā, Āśvina śukla 6–10 (Ṣaṣṭhī to Daśamī), preceded by Mahālayā on the amāvāsyā that ends the previous month (amānta Bhādrapada kṛṣṇa 15 = pūrṇimānta Āśvina kṛṣṇa 15) — so the eastern festival begins on the sixth night, not the first, and its own preliminary marker sits in the preceding lunation. Gujarat keeps the nine nights as garbā; Karnataka and Tamil Nadu keep Dasara/Golu, with Sarasvatī Pūjā aligned to Mūlā nakṣatra and Āyudha Pūjā on navamī. IMPLEMENTATION CAVEATS: (1) the nine days are nine tithis, so a kṣaya compresses the run to eight Gregorian days and a vṛddhi extends it to ten — `days: 9` is nominal, and the span must be generated tithi-by-tithi. (2) ADHIKA MĀSA MATTERS HERE MORE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE IN THIS CORPUS: when an adhika Āśvina intervenes the whole festival waits for nija Āśvina. This happened in 2020, when Durgā Pūjā fell in late October rather than September — a full lunation's displacement, and the standard way festival software fails.

name: Vijayadaśamī (Dussehra)
summary: The tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, closing Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā as the day of victory.
note:
Āśvina śukla daśamī; both reckonings agree. Kept in the APARĀHṆA, and the vijaya muhūrta proper is a short window within it — so when daśamī overlaps navamī or ekādaśī awkwardly, the aparāhṇa rule decides the day, and Vijayadaśamī is therefore NOT invariably the Gregorian day after the ninth day of Navarātri. Implementations that compute it as 'Navarātri start + 9 days' will be wrong in tithi-vṛddhi and tithi-kṣaya years; compute the daśamī independently. The older Kṣatriya content of the day is śamī-pūjana and sīmollaṅghana, the ceremonial crossing of the border to begin the campaigning season after the rains. Modern regional forms diverge sharply in content while sharing the tithi: Rāmlīlā and the burning of Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa and Meghanāda effigies in the north; the immersion of Durgā in the east; Āyudha Pūjā, Vidyārambha and the Mysore Dasara procession in the south. Like Śāradīya Navarātri, deferred to nija Āśvina when an adhika Āśvina intervenes.

name: Karva Chauth (Karaka Caturthī)
summary: A day-long waterless fast kept by married women, broken on sighting the moon on the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight before the Dīpāvalī new moon.
note:
THE CANONICAL TRAP OF THIS CORPUS. Every source names it Kārtika kṛṣṇa caturthī, because the vrata is kept almost exclusively in PŪRṆIMĀNTA regions — Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan, western Uttar Pradesh, Himachal, Jammu, Madhya Pradesh, and among Hindus in Nepal. That same day is amānta ĀŚVINA kṛṣṇa 4. Software that stores the popular name 'Kārtika kṛṣṇa 4' and evaluates it against an amānta calendar lands a full lunation late. The anchor here is amānta, with the pūrṇimānta name — the one users will actually type — recorded as a variant. Positionally: four days after the Āśvina/Kārtika full moon, and about nine days before Dīpāvalī. The fast runs from before sunrise and is broken only after sighting the moon through a sieve, so the observance is tied to MOONRISE on the caturthī evening, which is late — typically well after dark — and varies by longitude enough that published moonrise times differ across a single state. TEXTUAL CAVEAT: there is no secure classical Purāṇic locus for this vrata. Its kathā circulates in vernacular vrata-kathā literature and the Sanskrit name Karaka-caturthī appears only in later nibandha material; it is properly described as a regional women's observance of the medieval-to-modern period, and entries claiming Purāṇic authority for it are overreaching. Distinct from the monthly Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī, which shares the tithi type. Andhra's Atlā Taddi is a comparable women's observance but on a different tithi (Āśvina kṛṣṇa tṛtīyā) and must not be merged with it.

CAVEAT: kept until MOONRISE, not sunrise — the fast breaks on sighting the Moon. The engine has no moonrise day-rule; this entry will resolve to the sunrise answer, which is usually but not always the same day.

name: Dīpāvalī (Diwali)
summary: The five-day festival of lights spanning the new moon that ends the autumn lunation, from Dhanteras through Bhāī Dūj.
note: Umbrella entry; the five days are also given individually. The sequence is anchored at its FIRST day, Dhanteras, not at the principal day — Lakṣmī Pūjā on the amāvāsyā is day three. THE STRUCTURAL POINT implementers miss: days 1–3 lie in kṛṣṇa pakṣa and therefore split by reckoning (amānta Āśvina / pūrṇimānta Kārtika), while days 4–5 are Kārtika śukla 1 and 2 in BOTH systems. So under amānta reckoning the festival crosses a month boundary — Āśvina ends at the amāvāsyā and Kārtika begins the next morning — and under pūrṇimānta reckoning it does not. Any implementation that hard-codes 'Dīpāvalī = Kārtika amāvāsyā' and evaluates it amāntically will land one lunation late; the amānta name for the principal day is Āśvina amāvāsyā, which is exactly what Gujarati almanacs call it (Āso Vad Amās). CAVEAT ON DURATION: because tithis suffer kṣaya and vṛddhi, the five observances sometimes collapse into four Gregorian days or spread across six — Dhanteras and Naraka Caturdaśī, or Naraka Caturdaśī and Lakṣmī Pūjā, share a date in some years — so `days: 5` counts tithis, not calendar days. Regional and sectarian overlays on the same nights: Kālī Pūjā in Bengal, Assam and Odisha; Bandi Chhoṛ Divas in Sikhism; the Jain observance of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa on the amāvāsyā; and in Tamil Nadu the main day is Naraka Caturdaśī, not the amāvāsyā.

name: Dhanteras (Dhanatrayodaśī)
summary: First day of Dīpāvalī, on the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight, kept for Dhanvantari and for the lamp offered to Yama.
note:
RECKONING SPLIT: amānta Āśvina kṛṣṇa 13 = pūrṇimānta Kārtika kṛṣṇa 13. Same day; the anchor is amānta and the northern name is recorded as a variant. Also Dhanvantari Trayodaśī, the appearance day of the physician-deity who emerged from the churning of the ocean bearing the pot of amṛta — the Government of India has kept it as National Ayurveda Day since 2016. Lakṣmī and Kubera pūjā in pradoṣa kāla, after sunset, so the day kept is decided by which evening carries the trayodaśī. Yama Dīpam: a lamp set at the threshold facing south after dusk, for Yama — in some pañcāṅgas this is reckoned separately from the Dhanvantari observance and can fall on the adjacent day when trayodaśī is short. The purchase of metal is customary; its present commercial scale is modern.

name: Naraka Caturdaśī (Choṭī Dīwālī / Kālī Caudas)
summary: Second day of Dīpāvalī, on the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight, marking the killing of Narakāsura and kept with a ritual pre-dawn bath.
note: RECKONING SPLIT: amānta Āśvina kṛṣṇa 14 = pūrṇimānta Kārtika kṛṣṇa 14. Same day; anchor is amānta. TIMING SUBTLETY: the abhyaṅga snāna, the oil bath, is prescribed before sunrise in aruṇodaya — the pre-dawn twilight — so the day kept is decided by whether caturdaśī is current at DAWN rather than at sunrise proper. This regularly separates the 'bath day' from the 'Choṭī Dīwālī evening' in published pañcāṅgas, which is why some almanacs list the two on different dates in the same year. Not an error; two different rules. In Tamil Nadu and much of the south this day, not the amāvāsyā, is the principal Dīpāvalī, kept with the pre-dawn oil bath and new clothes. CLOSED MATERIAL: in Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan the night is Kālī Caudas, carrying tantric and apotropaic observance and, in some lineages, initiatory practice. That material is not published in detail here, and this entry is deliberately limited to the public calendrical facts.

name: Lakṣmī Pūjā (Dīpāvalī Amāvāsyā)
summary: The principal night of Dīpāvalī, on the new moon that closes the autumn lunation, kept with lamps and the worship of Lakṣmī and Gaṇeśa.
note:
RECKONING SPLIT, and the one that matters most: amānta ĀŚVINA amāvāsyā = pūrṇimānta KĀRTIKA amāvāsyā. Because an amānta month ENDS at the new moon, this night is the last day of amānta Āśvina, and Gujarati almanacs accordingly call it Āso Vad Amās — while northern almanacs call the identical night Kārtika Amāvāsyā. The near-universal software error is to store 'Kārtika amāvāsyā' and resolve it amāntically, which yields a date one lunation late. Anchor is amānta; the northern name is a variant. TIMING: pūjā is performed in pradoṣa kāla after sunset, ideally in a sthira (fixed) lagna, so the night kept is the one on whose EVENING amāvāsyā prevails — which is not always the day on which amāvāsyā is current at sunrise. Merchants open new account books (cāupaḍā pūjan in Gujarat). GENUINE INTRA-NIGHT DIVERGENCE: in Bengal, Assam and Odisha the same new moon is Kālī Pūjā / Śyāmā Pūjā, but kept at NIŚĪTHA (midnight) rather than pradoṣa; when the amāvāsyā spans two evenings, the pradoṣa and niśītha rules can select different Gregorian dates, so Lakṣmī Pūjā and Kālī Pūjā occasionally fall on different days. Also the Jain Dīpāvalī, marking Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa at Pāvāpurī. In Gujarat and Maharashtra this is the last day of the outgoing Vikrama year.

name: Govardhana Pūjā (Annakūṭa / Bali Pratipadā)
summary: Fourth day of Dīpāvalī, on the first lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, offering a mountain of food before Govardhana.
note: Kārtika śukla pratipadā. Śukla pakṣa, so amānta and pūrṇimānta AGREE on the month — the reckoning split that governs the first three days of Dīpāvalī stops here. Annakūṭa, 'mountain of food', traditionally fifty-six offerings (chappan bhog), presented before a Govardhana modelled in cow dung; the narrative is Kṛṣṇa's lifting of the hill against Indra's rains. Central to Puṣṭimārga, Gauḍīya and Svāminārāyaṇa practice, and the day of the Govardhana parikramā at Mathurā. In Maharashtra, Gujarat and the Konkan the same day is Bali Pratipadā, commemorating Vāmana's suppression of Bali — a different narrative on the same tithi. CALENDRICAL CONSEQUENCE worth encoding: in Gujarat this is Beṣṭu Varas, the new year, and the Vikrama Saṃvat number increments HERE (Kārttikādi reckoning), whereas in the pūrṇimānta north the Vikrama year turns at Chaitra śukla 1 (Chaitrādi). Gujarati and North Indian Vikrama year numbers are therefore out of step by one for the stretch between Kārtika śukla 1 and Chaitra śukla 1 — a standard source of error in date conversion. When a tithi kṣaya removes pratipadā, Govardhana Pūjā and Bhāī Dūj can fall on the same Gregorian day.

name: Bhāī Dūj (Yama Dvitīyā)
summary: Fifth and final day of Dīpāvalī, on the second lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, on which sisters honour their brothers.
note: Kārtika śukla dvitīyā; śukla pakṣa, so both reckonings agree on the month. Observed in the aparāhṇa. The frame narrative is Yamunā receiving her brother Yama at her house and marking his forehead, whence the name Yama Dvitīyā; bathing in the Yamunā on this day is the older prescription. NEPAL CAVEAT: Bhāi Ṭīkā is fixed by the Nepali pañcāṅga and is frequently kept a day later than the Indian date; record it as its own observance rather than aliasing it. Distinct from Rakṣā Bandhan despite the shared sibling theme — different month, different tithi, different rite; the two are conflated constantly in secondary descriptions and should be kept separate in data. name: Kārtika Pūrṇimā
summary: The full moon of Kārtika, closing the month's observances and kept as Tripurī Pūrṇimā and Dev Dīpāvalī.
note: Kārtika śukla 15; both reckonings agree, this being a pūrṇimā. Closes the Kārtika-vrata — the month of pre-dawn bathing, lamp offering and tulasī worship whose māhātmya occupies large sections of the Padma and Skanda Purāṇas. Also Tripurī or Tripurārī Pūrṇimā, commemorating Śiva's destruction of the three cities. Kept as Dev Dīpāvalī, most spectacularly on the Vārāṇasī ghāṭs. Cāturmāsya ends and Vaiṣṇava marriages resume — though note the reckoning caveat under Guru Pūrṇimā: traditions that start the retreat at Devaśayanī Ekādaśī end it at Prabodhinī Ekādaśī (Kārtika śukla 11), four days earlier, rather than here. The Pushkar cattle and camel fair concludes on this day. SIKH OVERLAY WITH A SCHOLARLY CAVEAT: the day is kept as Gurū Nānak's Gurpurab, but the assignment of Nānak's birth to Kārtika Pūrṇimā derives from the later Bhāī Bālā janamsākhī tradition, while the older Purātan tradition places the birth in Vaisākh; historians of the Sikh tradition, W. H. McLeod among them, regard the Kārtika date as historically insecure even though it is the universal observance. Record the observance, not the historicity. Kārttikai Dīpam in Tamil Nadu is related but is fixed to Kṛttikā nakṣatra within the Tamil solar month of Kārttikai, so it can fall a day off the North Indian pūrṇimā.

name: Śukla Pakṣa Ekādaśī
summary: The eleventh tithi of the waxing fortnight, kept as a fast to Viṣṇu in every lunar month.
note: Recurs every lunation; the anchor month is a wildcard ("*"), not a single month. Śukla-pakṣa tithis carry the same month name in both amānta and pūrṇimānta reckoning, so no reckoning field is needed. WHAT IS DONE: a fast (upavāsa) from the daśamī evening meal through ekādaśī, Viṣṇu-pūjā, night vigil (jāgara), and pāraṇa (breaking the fast) the next morning on dvādaśī. Graded relaxations are textually sanctioned for those unable to fast absolutely — ekabhakta (one meal after midday), nakta, phalāhāra, milk — but Manu XI.30 and Kane's discussion insist these are for the incapable only. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: this is the single most contested nirṇaya in the whole corpus and MBF has no field for it. Ekādaśī is exempted from the ordinary udaya-vyāpinī rule. A tithi is pūrṇa only if it runs 60 ghaṭikās from sunrise to sunrise; Garuḍa and Bhaviṣya add that ekādaśī counts as pūrṇa only if it also exists two muhūrtas (4 ghaṭikās, ~96 min) BEFORE that sunrise. If daśamī persists into those last 4 ghaṭikās there is aruṇodaya-vedha; if daśamī is still running at the instant of sunrise there is sūryodaya-vedha. The yugmavākya pairing rule independently prefers ekādaśī joined to dvādaśī and condemns ekādaśī joined to daśamī (Nāradapurāṇa pūrvārdha 29.39–40; the Gāndhārī verse). Where two consecutive days both carry ekādaśī, Nāradapurāṇa 29.45 gives householders the earlier and yatis/sannyāsins the later. ADHIKA MĀSA: this entry is not observed in an intercalary month under its ordinary name — but see adhika-masa-ekadashi, which is the explicit exception, since the adhika month's two ekādaśīs have their own names and are observed.

regionalVariants.note: Smārtas — meaning all who are not initiated Vaiṣṇavas — are unaffected by aruṇodaya-vedha and are bound only by sūryodaya-vedha. If daśamī ends before sunrise and ekādaśī runs from sunrise, the Smārta fasts that day. Smārtas may also fast on an ekādaśī viddha by daśamī when dvādaśī does not exist at all on the thirteenth tithi; Vaiṣṇavas may not.

anchor.condition: only when the ekādaśī is viddha by aruṇodaya- or sūryodaya-vedha

regionalVariants.note: An initiated Vaiṣṇava cannot fast on an ekādaśī preceded by aruṇodaya-vedha even if that ekādaśī is otherwise a full 60-ghaṭikā tithi. The fast moves to the day wholly covered by dvādaśī and pāraṇa moves to the day after, when dvādaśī ends. This is why Vaiṣṇava and Smārta pañcāṅgas routinely print ekādaśī on different civil dates, often labelled 'Vaiṣṇava Ekādaśī'. Kane notes the practical consequence: to complete pāraṇa before dvādaśī expires, observants rise well before dawn and compress the morning rites. The strict Vaiṣṇava rules presuppose āgamic dīkṣā (Vaikhānasa, Pāñcarātra); the dīkṣā rites themselves are restricted, but the ekādaśī observance is public.

name: Kṛṣṇa Pakṣa Ekādaśī
summary: The eleventh tithi of the waning fortnight, kept as a fast to Viṣṇu in every lunar month.
note: Recurs every lunation; wildcard month. RECKONING: for any single occurrence the month name differs between systems — a kṛṣṇa pakṣa that amānta calls month M is called month M+1 by pūrṇimānta reckoning. Kane states this directly as the cause of the divergence in the traditional list of 24 ekādaśī names: what is Bhādra-kṛṣṇa in pūrṇimānta is Śrāvaṇa-kṛṣṇa in amānta, and the Purāṇas are not consistent about which system they use. Because this entry's month is a wildcard the two systems cover the same set of days, so no reckoning field is set; any derived single-date entry MUST set one. ADHIKĀRA — this is the substantive difference from the śukla ekādaśī and it is not a minor one: the kṛṣṇa ekādaśī fast is NOT obligatory for householders. Devala restricts the householder to the śukla ekādaśī alone; Padmapurāṇa permits him the kṛṣṇa ekādaśīs falling between Śayanī and Bodhinī (the cāturmāsya) and no others; Nārada goes further and says a householder who has a son should not fast on kṛṣṇa ekādaśī, on a saṅkrānti, or at an eclipse. A widow is treated as a yati; a woman whose husband is living fasts only in the śukla pakṣa. None of these restrictions bind initiated Vaiṣṇavas, for whom both pakṣas are nitya. Hemādri dissented from the whole restriction and held that all persons have adhikāra in both pakṣas. Do not flatten this into 'everyone fasts twice a month' — the texts genuinely disagree about who is entitled. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: identical to the śukla ekādaśī (see that entry) — vedha by daśamī, not plain udaya-vyāpti, decides the civil day.

regionalVariants.note: Obligatory in both pakṣas without restriction. Skandapurāṇa's working definition of a Vaiṣṇava is precisely one who does not forsake the ekādaśī fast.

name: Kṛṣṇa Pradoṣa
summary: The thirteenth tithi of the waning fortnight, worshipped to Śiva in the twilight hour after sunset.
note:
Recurs every lunation; wildcard month, so no reckoning field (for a single dated occurrence the kṛṣṇa pakṣa takes different month names in the two systems). WHAT IS DONE: a fast broken after sunset; bath about an hour before sunset; worship of Śiva with abhiṣeka, bilva leaves, sandal, dīpa and naivedya, together with Pārvatī, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya and Nandi; in South Indian temples Nandi is worshipped and the utsava-mūrti of Śiva with Pārvatī is taken in procession on the vṛṣabha-vāhana; the Pradoṣa story is read after the pūjā. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP — THIS ENTRY IS THE CLEAREST COUNTER-EXAMPLE IN THE CORPUS: the ordinary sunrise rule does not select the day. Pradoṣa requires trayodaśī to be current during pradoṣa-kāla, the twilight window after sunset, so the observed civil day is frequently one whose tithi AT SUNRISE is dvādaśī. Any implementation that assigns Pradoṣa by sunrise tithi will be wrong roughly half the time. THE WINDOW ITSELF IS DISPUTED: Dharmasindhu p. 9 defines it as sūryāstottaraṃ trimuhūrtaḥ pradoṣaḥ — the three muhūrtas (~144 minutes) after sunset. Widely circulated modern usage instead gives a three-hour window straddling sunset (90 minutes either side), and other authorities give shorter spans. These do not always select the same day; where they differ, record the range rather than picking one. The yugmavākya pairing rule does not cover the thirteenth tithi of either pakṣa, but the express supplementary rule at the same locus prefers kṛṣṇa trayodaśī joined to the FOLLOWING caturdaśī. WEEKDAY VARIANTS: Pradoṣa on Saturday is Śani Pradoṣa, held the most important, with a strong association to Mahākāleśvara at Ujjain; on Monday, Soma Pradoṣa. These are conditions on the weekday, which MBF has no field for.

name: Śukla Pradoṣa
summary: The thirteenth tithi of the waxing fortnight, worshipped to Śiva in the twilight hour after sunset.
note:
The waxing-fortnight member of the pair; identical in rite and in timing rule to Kṛṣṇa Pradoṣa, and recorded separately only because MBF's lunar anchor takes a single paksha. Śukla tithis are named identically in both reckonings, so no reckoning field. The Purāṇic definition Kane reports — that pradoṣa is the junction where trayodaśī meets the end of dvādaśī at twilight — applies in both fortnights. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: as with the kṛṣṇa member, the day is chosen by trayodaśī prevailing during pradoṣa-kāla after sunset, not by the tithi at sunrise; the window's extent is disputed (see the kṛṣṇa entry). The yugmavākya does not govern the thirteenth tithi of either fortnight, and Kane notes that combinations of the 12th with the 13th, and of the 13th with the 14th, are among those generally excluded as improper — so the day must be settled by the pradoṣa-vyāpti criterion rather than by pairing.

Day rule: pradoṣa — the vrata is by definition kept at pradoṣa.

name: Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī
summary: The fourth tithi of the waning fortnight, fasted to Gaṇeśa and broken only after sighting the moon.
note: Recurs every lunation; wildcard month. For a single dated occurrence the month name differs by reckoning — the Māgha kṛṣṇa caturthī of amānta reckoning is the Phālguna kṛṣṇa caturthī of pūrṇimānta — so any derived entry must set one. WHAT IS DONE: a strict daytime fast, Gaṇeśa-pūjā, recitation of the Gaṇapati Atharvaśīrṣa before moonrise, and arghya offered to Candra; the fast is broken at night only AFTER darśana of the moon. Kane's vrata-list records the rite as Saṅkaṣṭahara-Gaṇapati-vrata, on Māgha kṛṣṇa 4, expressly classed as a tithivrata at moonrise, with Vratarāja's elaborate procedure (Gaṇeśa worshipped with 21 dūrvā, 108 and 21 names, five modakas to the priest); Vyāsa is said to narrate it to Yudhiṣṭhira. Each month's observance has its own name of Gaṇeśa, its own pīṭha and its own vrata-kathā, and — significantly — the cycle includes a thirteenth story for the intercalary month. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP — CRITICAL AND USUALLY GOT WRONG: the determining moment is candrodaya, not sunrise. Because a kṛṣṇa caturthī moon rises late in the evening, the day on which caturthī is current AT MOONRISE is very often the day AFTER the day that carries caturthī at sunrise. Implementations that assign this by sunrise tithi produce a one-day error for a large fraction of months. WEEKDAY VARIANT: falling on a Tuesday it is Aṅgārakī (Aṅgāraka) Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī, held the most efficacious of the year; the legend attaches it to Māgha kṛṣṇa caturthī on a Tuesday. MBF has no weekday-condition field. The Māgha occurrence is separately known in North and Central India as Sakaṭ Chauth.

name: Vināyaka Caturthī
summary: The fourth tithi of the waxing fortnight, worshipped to Gaṇeśa at midday.
note: Recurs every lunation; wildcard month. Śukla tithis are named alike in both reckonings, so no reckoning field. Also called Varada Caturthī (Samayamayūkha). Distinguish sharply from Saṅkaṣṭī, which is the kṛṣṇa-pakṣa caturthī with a moonrise rule; these are two different observances with two different timing criteria and are routinely conflated. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: the governing moment is madhyāhna (midday), stated by Bṛhaspati as quoted in Mādhava's Kālanirṇaya. Kane uses precisely this vrata to illustrate that one and the same tithi may be preferred pūrva-viddhā in one case and para-viddhā in another: if caturthī is current at midday and then runs into pañcamī, but was NOT current at midday the previous day, take the caturthī joined to pañcamī; if instead it is joined to tṛtīyā before noon and is not current at midday, take the caturthī joined to tṛtīyā. This is a real conditional, not a preference, and MBF has no field for it. The yugmavākya independently pairs 4 with 5. A separate prohibition attaches to the Bhādrapada śukla caturthī: seeing the moon that night incurs a false accusation, remedied by reciting the nurse's verse over water and hearing the Syamantaka story (Tithitattva); this is why the annual Gaṇeśa Caturthī and the monthly Vināyaka Caturthī carry opposite instructions about looking at the moon — the monthly Saṅkaṣṭī REQUIRES moon-darśana, this one forbids it in Bhādrapada.

name: Māsa Śivarātri
summary: The fourteenth tithi of the waning fortnight, kept as a night vigil to Śiva in every lunar month.
note:
CONFIDENCE IS 'reconstructed' DELIBERATELY. The nibandha literature treats Śivarātri principally as a single annual observance — the caturdaśī of Māgha kṛṣṇa in pūrṇimānta reckoning, which is Phālguna kṛṣṇa 14 in amānta reckoning (Īśānasaṃhitā, Nāgarakhaṇḍa as quoted by Hemādri). The monthly generalisation rests on the fact that the governing Skandapurāṇa verse is stated generically — 'a fast should be observed on that caturdaśī of the dark half that is joined to niśītha' — without naming a month, and on Āgamic and pañcāṅga usage. I have not found the monthly recurrence asserted at a nibandha locus, so the anchor is derived rather than directly attested. WHAT IS DONE: a fast, and worship of Śiva at night rather than by day, since (Skanda) the bhūtas, śaktis and Śiva himself move at night; a jāgara through the night. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: none of the criteria is sunrise. Mādhava's cascade, which Kane calls the conclusion of the prince of nirṇayakāras, runs: (1) if caturdaśī covers both pradoṣa and niśītha, that is the day; (2) if it spreads over two days and covers niśītha on both or on neither, pradoṣa-coverage decides; (3) if it covers pradoṣa on both or on neither, niśītha decides; (4) if each of the two days covers exactly one of pradoṣa and niśītha, conjunction with trayodaśī (Jayā) decides. Sources genuinely split on which term is primary: Nirṇayāmṛta stresses pradoṣa, others stress niśītha and ardharātra; Hemādri, Kālanirṇaya, Tithitattva, Nirṇayasindhu and Puruṣārthacintāmaṇi each discuss it at length. Record the cascade, not a single rule.

Day rule: niśītha — the monthly Śivarātri follows the same midnight rule.

name: Kālāṣṭamī
summary: The eighth tithi of the waning fortnight, kept to Bhairava in every lunar month.
note:
CONFIDENCE IS 'reconstructed'. Kane's list of vratas records Kālabhairavāṣṭamī as an annual tithivrata on Mārgaśīrṣa kṛṣṇa 8 with Kālabhairava as deity; the MONTHLY observance of every kṛṣṇa aṣṭamī as Kālāṣṭamī is standard in current pañcāṅgas and in Bhairava temple practice but I could not source the monthly recurrence to a nibandha locus. The annual Mārgaśīrṣa occurrence is the well-attested one and is often called Kālabhairava Jayantī. WHAT IS DONE: fast and night worship of Bhairava; in temple practice, offerings at the Bhairava shrine and, at some sites, feeding of dogs as Bhairava's vāhana. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: the yugmavākya pairs 8 with 9, and the express supplementary rule at the same locus puts the eighth tithi among those preferred in combination with the FOLLOWING tithi — i.e. aṣṭamī is taken para-viddhā, joined to navamī, not pūrva-viddhā joined to saptamī. Kane notes this is overridden where an express text intervenes: in Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī the fast is kept on the aṣṭamī conjoined with Rohiṇī even where that means taking it with the seventh tithi against the yugmavākya. For a night-worship observance such as Kālāṣṭamī the practical criterion in current use is niśītha-vyāpti, parallel to Śivarātri; I record that as usage rather than as an attested rule.

Day rule: niśītha — Bhairava worship kept at midnight.

name: Ṣaṣṭhī (Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī)
summary: The sixth tithi of the waxing fortnight, kept to Skanda–Murugan in every lunar month.
note: CONFIDENCE IS 'reconstructed' for the monthly recurrence. Kane attests the vrata and, importantly, its distinctive nirṇaya rule, but treats the great annual Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī (Aippasi/Kārtika) as the principal observance; the monthly Ṣaṣṭhī is Tamil temple practice, especially at the six padai vīdu shrines. Śukla tithis are named alike in both reckonings, so no reckoning field. WHAT IS DONE: fast, worship of Skanda–Murugan, recitation of the Kanda Ṣaṣṭhī Kavacam in Tamil practice; at the annual observance a six-day fast culminating in the Sūrasaṃhāram. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: Kane uses this vrata as his textbook illustration that the deity, not the tithi number, can decide the viddha-preference — Skandaṣaṣṭhī is preferred PŪRVA-VIDDHĀ, that is, taken joined to the preceding pañcamī, whereas Mandāraṣaṣṭhī, the same sixth tithi, is preferred PARA-VIDDHĀ because its deity is Mandāra and not Skanda. This directly contradicts the yugmavākya's own supplementary rule, which places the sixth tithi among those preferred joined to the following seventh; Kane's point is that an express text defeats the general pairing. Two observances on the same tithi number can therefore fall on different civil days.

name: Amāvāsyā
summary: The new moon, the fifteenth tithi of the waning fortnight, kept for offerings to the ancestors.
note: Recurs every lunation; wildcard month. The amānta lunar month ENDS on amāvāsyā; the pūrṇimānta month has its midpoint there. Because the month is a wildcard no reckoning field is set, but any dated occurrence must set one. WHAT IS DONE: darśa-śrāddha and tarpaṇa to the pitṛs, pinda offered with sesame and ghee, bathing at a tīrtha, and a fast. Amāvāsyā is the pitṛ-tithi par excellence and its rites are the monthly counterpart of the annual Mahālaya. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP — TWO DIFFERENT RULES APPLY DEPENDING ON THE RITE, AND THEY CAN SELECT DIFFERENT DAYS: (1) For śrāddha and tarpaṇa the criterion is aparāhṇa-vyāpti. Manu III.278 prescribes aparāhṇa for śrāddha; Prajāpati-smṛti 156–157 fixes aparāhṇa as the fourth of five parts of a fifteen-muhūrta day, each of three muhūrtas, and adds that śrāddha should begin in the kutapa muhūrta (the eighth from sunrise) and not run past the twelfth, five muhūrtas being the maximum. Crucially, Kane records that rites for the pitṛs are NOT governed by the yugmavākya at all: the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa holds that the pitṛs attend upon the tithi current AT SUNSET, and that this tithi and the afternoon were assigned to the pitṛs by Brahmā. (2) For amāvāsyā vratas other than pitṛ-rites the yugmavākya applies, pairing amāvāsyā with the following pratipadā: Kane's vrata-list states that amāvāsyā mixed with the first tithi is to be preferred to one mixed with the fourteenth — with an express exception for Sāvitrī-vrata. Do not collapse these into one rule. WEEKDAY: an amāvāsyā falling on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday is held specially holy, as is one falling on Anurādhā, Viśākhā or Svātī nakṣatra — see somavati-amavasya.

name: Somavatī Amāvāsyā
summary: A new moon that falls on a Monday, held especially efficacious for ancestral rites and for married women's vows.
note: A weekday-conditional occurrence of amāvāsyā, not a fixed calendar date: it happens only when the amāvāsyā-owning civil day is a Monday, so it occurs a few times a year at irregular intervals and in some years not at all. MBF has no weekday-condition field, so the condition is carried in an extra anchor key and must not be read as a fixed monthly event. TEXTUAL BASIS: Kane's vrata-list records, citing the Varṣakriyākaumudī quoting the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas, that an amāvāsyā falling on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday is specially holy, as also one falling on Anurādhā, Viśākhā or Svātī nakṣatra. Note that the older texts privilege THREE weekdays; the modern cult has singled out Monday alone and attached it to Śiva through the Monday–Soma–Candra association. The Tuesday and Thursday members of the same rule have no comparable modern observance. Treat 'Somavatī' as a later specialisation of a broader attested rule rather than as the rule itself. WHAT IS DONE: bathing at a tīrtha, tarpaṇa to the pitṛs, and in North Indian practice a fast by married women with circumambulation of an aśvattha tree for their husbands' welfare and pūjā to Śiva. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits amāvāsyā's rules — aparāhṇa-vyāpti for the pitṛ-rites, the amāvāsyā-plus-pratipadā pairing otherwise. The weekday is that of the civil day so selected, which means a vṛddhi of amāvāsyā across two days can make the Monday and the ritually-owning day come apart; sources do not settle this case.

name: Pūrṇimā
summary: The full moon, the fifteenth tithi of the waxing fortnight, kept with fasting, bathing and worship.
note: Recurs every lunation; wildcard month. The pūrṇimānta lunar month ENDS on pūrṇimā; the amānta month has its midpoint there. Śukla tithis are named alike in both systems, so no reckoning field is needed even for dated occurrences — pūrṇimā is the one tithi on which the two reckonings never disagree about the month name, though they disagree about whether it closes the month or falls mid-month. WHAT IS DONE: a fast, bathing at a tīrtha, Satyanārāyaṇa-pūjā in much of North India and Maharashtra (see satyanarayana-purnima and its caveat), and in several months a major annual festival (Guru Pūrṇimā in Āṣāḍha, Rakṣā Bandhan in Śrāvaṇa, Kojāgarī in Āśvina, Kārtika Pūrṇimā, Holikā in Phālguna). SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: the yugmavākya pairs the fourteenth tithi with pūrṇimā and excludes the pairing of pūrṇimā with the following pratipadā, so pūrṇimā is ordinarily preferred PŪRVA-VIDDHĀ — taken on the day where it is joined to the preceding caturdaśī. This is the reverse of amāvāsyā, which is preferred para-viddhā joined to pratipadā, and the asymmetry is deliberate in the text. But the general fallback verse cited by Kālanirṇaya cuts the other way for the dark fortnight — 'in the bright half prefer the tithi current at sunrise; in the dark half, the tithi current at sunset' — and pūrṇimās whose rite is a night observance (Kojāgarī, Holikā) are settled by the tithi prevailing at night rather than at sunrise. Where a pūrṇimā spans two sunrises the fast day and the night-worship day can therefore separate; record both rather than choosing.

name: Satyanārāyaṇa Pūjā (Pūrṇimā)
summary: Household worship of Viṣṇu as Satyanārāyaṇa, customarily performed on the full moon.
note: MARKED DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE IS ABOUT THE DATE ITSELF. The near-universal modern association with pūrṇimā is CUSTOM, NOT TEXT. Kane's summary of the vrata, drawn from the Purāṇic and nibandha material, opens with the words 'On any day a man worships Satyanārāyaṇa' — the sources he collects impose no tithi. The pūrṇimā anchoring, and the secondary preference for Kārtika and Vaiśākha pūrṇimā, come from later household usage, not from a prescriptive locus. Any pack that prints this as a fixed pūrṇimā observance is over-claiming. TEXTUAL PROVENANCE IS ALSO CONTESTED: the vrata is described in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, Pratisargaparva chs. 24–29, and occurs in the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa in the Vaṅgavāsī edition but NOT in the Veṅkaṭeśvara Press edition — a recension difference that bears directly on its antiquity. Mahāmahopādhyāya Hara Prasad Shastri, cataloguing the Asiatic Society manuscripts, argued the worship was originally Satya Pīr'er pūjā and of Muslim origin, adopted into Bengali Hindu practice, the offering of sirṇi to Satya Pīr becoming the naivedya of Satyanārāyaṇa. That claim is disputed but must be recorded. WHAT IS DONE: naivedya of savā (one and a quarter measures) of plantain, ghee, milk and wheat or rice flour with jaggery, mixed together; recitation of the five kathās; jāgara with song and dance; distribution of prasāda. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: since no tithi is textually prescribed, none applies; where pūrṇimā is followed, it inherits pūrṇimā's rules.

name: Saṅkrānti
summary: The sun's passage from one sidereal zodiacal sign into the next, occurring twelve times a year and opening each solar month.
note: THE FRAME IS SIDEREAL, NOT TROPICAL — this is the single most important technical caveat and MBF's solar anchor has no field for it. Hindu saṅkrānti is nirayana: Meṣa Saṅkrānti is the sun's entry into sidereal Aries, which falls around 14 April, not at the March equinox, the gap being the ayanāṃśa of roughly 24 degrees. Different ayanāṃśas in use (Lahiri/Chitrapakṣa, Raman, Krishnamurti) differ by up to about a degree, which is enough to move a saṅkrānti across a civil day boundary. Any consumer reading degrees:0 as a tropical equinox will be about three weeks wrong. PUṆYA-KĀLA — the moment of transit is instantaneous and unobservable, so a window around it is used, and the window is NOT uniform. The general limit is thirty ghaṭikās either side, with a holiest core of three to twelve ghaṭikās; Ṣaḍaśīti saṅkrāntis allow sixty, Viṣṇupadī sixteen. Dharmasindhu's working conclusions, which Kane summarises, are sign-specific: Meṣa and Tulā, fifteen ghaṭikās either side (some say ten); Vṛṣabha, Siṃha, Vṛścika, Kumbha, sixteen ghaṭikās BEFORE; Mithuna, Kanyā, Dhanus, Mīna, sixteen ghaṭikās AFTER; Karka, thirty after; Makara, forty after. NIGHT TRANSITS: if the saṅkrānti falls by day the whole day is puṇyakāla. If it falls at night, for the ten signs other than Makara and Karka the puṇyakāla is taken by day; before midnight, the latter half of the preceding daytime; at or after midnight, split across the latter half of the day before and the first half of the day after. For Makara at night the puṇyakāla is the following day, for Karka at night the preceding day; Makara at evening twilight takes the previous day, Karka in morning twilight the following day. WHAT IS DONE: bathing and dāna within the puṇyakāla. Nārada bars a householder with a son from fasting on a saṅkrānti.

I have not verified the precise thresholds against a primary source and do not state them; see Sewell and Dikshit.

name: Pitṛ Pakṣa (Mahālaya Pakṣa)
summary: The waning fortnight of Bhādrapada, set aside for śrāddha and tarpaṇa to the ancestors.
note:
MARKED DISPUTED BECAUSE THE START DATE AND LENGTH ARE GENUINELY UNSETTLED, NOT BECAUSE THE OBSERVANCE IS. Kane states plainly that various views are held on the exact day, and lists them: from the first tithi of the dark half of Bhādrapada to amāvāsyā; or from the fifth to amāvāsyā; or from the eighth or tenth to amāvāsyā; or from the fifth of the dark half to the fifth of the NEXT fortnight; or on any day while the sun is in Kanyā; or on any day until the sun enters Vṛścika. The universal label 'sixteen śrāddhas' does not fit kṛṣṇa pratipadā to amāvāsyā, which is fifteen tithis; Kane records a third construction that reaches sixteen by INCLUDING THE PRECEDING FULL MOON DAY along with the fifteen days of the dark half, and this is why many pañcāṅgas open Mahālaya on Bhādrapada Pūrṇimā while the first śrāddha proper is on pratipadā. I have anchored on kṛṣṇa pratipadā with lasts:16 and flag the one-day head as unresolved. The Padmapurāṇa defines the period as the fifth fortnight from the full moon of Āṣāḍha — which is Bhādrapada kṛṣṇa — and ties it to the sun standing in Kanyā, adding that if it cannot be done then it may be done while the sun is in Tulā, but that when the sun enters Vṛścika the pitṛs depart cursing. RECKONING MATTERS HERE: amānta Bhādrapada kṛṣṇa is pūrṇimānta Āśvina kṛṣṇa; both name the same fortnight. SPECIAL DAYS: caturthī and pañcamī (Chautha Bharaṇī, Bharaṇī Pañcamī) for those dead within the year; the day the moon stands in Bharaṇī is Mahābharaṇī, whose śrāddha the Matsyapurāṇa equates to Gayāśrāddha; navamī (Avidhavā Navamī) for women predeceasing their husbands; dvādaśī reserved for sannyāsins, and Kane notes this is the ONLY tithi on which a yati's mahālaya may be done, because dvādaśī is sacred to Viṣṇu; caturdaśī (Ghāta Caturdaśī) for those violently killed. ADHIKA MĀSA: Kane states expressly that the Mahālayaśrāddha is not to be performed in an intercalary month. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: aparāhṇa, per the general śrāddha rule; the pitṛ rites stand outside the yugmavākya and follow the tithi current at sunset.

Day rule: aparāhṇa — the fortnight's śrāddha rites are aparāhṇa rites.

name: Sarvapitṛ Amāvāsyā (Mahālaya Amāvāsyā)
summary: The new moon closing Pitṛ Pakṣa, on which śrāddha is offered to all ancestors regardless of their death-tithi.
note:
The final and most important day of Pitṛ Pakṣa. Also called Pitṛ Amāvāsyā, Peddala Amāvāsya, and in Bengal simply Mahālaya. RECKONING: amānta Bhādrapada kṛṣṇa 15 is pūrṇimānta Āśvina kṛṣṇa 15 — the same day under two month names. WHAT IS DONE: śrāddha for all ancestors irrespective of the lunar day on which they died, which is why it also serves as the remedy for a forgotten or neglected annual śrāddha. Pinda-dāna with rice, barley flour, ghee and black sesame; tarpaṇa; feeding of a cow, a dog and brāhmaṇas; the offering is held accepted when a crow takes the food. Kane records that on this day, and on the Mātāmaha śrāddha alone, a daughter's son may offer for the maternal line where no male heir survives. The Kalpataru, citing the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, provides that one who has missed Mahālaya may offer instead on the fourteenth of the dark half of Āśvina, the day on which lamps are lit. Pilgrimage to Gayā for pinda-dāna is concentrated in this fortnight. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP — THIS IS WHERE IT MATTERS MOST: aparāhṇa-vyāpti governs, not sunrise. The observed day is the one on which amāvāsyā is current during the fourth of the five parts of the day, with the rite begun in the kutapa muhūrta (the eighth from sunrise) and not extending past the twelfth. Because amāvāsyā frequently begins mid-morning or ends before midday, the aparāhṇa rule and the sunrise rule select DIFFERENT civil days several times a decade, and the pitṛ rites are expressly exempt from the yugmavākya that would otherwise pair amāvāsyā with pratipadā.

name: Nirjalā Ekādaśī
summary: The waterless ekādaśī of Jyeṣṭha, the most austere of the twenty-four and held to yield the merit of all of them.
note: Śukla tithis carry the same month name in both reckonings, so no reckoning field. Also called Pāṇḍava Nirjalā or Bhīmasenī Ekādaśī. WHAT IS DONE: an absolute fast without even water — Kane notes the vrata consists in not using or drinking water except at bathing or at ācamana, and the permitted quantity at ācamana is a single drop. Observed from sunrise on the ekādaśī to sunrise on the dvādaśī, though some hold sunrise to sunset. Viṣṇu or a śālagrāma is bathed in pañcāmṛta; dūrvā is offered in the evening; a night vigil is kept; and the characteristic dāna is of water-pots, fans, umbrellas and clothes — gifts fitted to the season, since the vrata falls in the hottest part of the Indian summer, which is exactly why the texts commend it so highly. LEGEND: Bhīma, unable to control his hunger through the other twenty-three, is advised by Vyāsa to keep this one and thereby obtains their combined merit. Kane records Hemādri quoting the MAHĀBHĀRATA for the vrata; the Brahmavaivartapurāṇa carries a version of the Bhīma narrative. The claim that it equals all twenty-four is a māhātmya claim, of the exaggerated kind Kane discusses at length, not a nirṇaya rule. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits the full ekādaśī apparatus — aruṇodaya-vedha and sūryodaya-vedha, the Smārta/Vaiṣṇava split, and pāraṇa on dvādaśī. See ekadashi-shukla.

name: Devśayanī (Śayanī) Ekādaśī
summary: The ekādaśī of Āṣāḍha on which Viṣṇu is held to begin his four-month sleep, opening Cāturmāsya.
note: Śukla, so no reckoning field. Also Mahā-Ekādaśī, Āṣāḍhī, Hariśayanī, Devaśayanī. Kane records the Garuḍapurāṇa's designation of the Āṣāḍha śukla ekādaśī as mahā-ekādaśī and as Śayanī, and pairs it explicitly with Prabodhinī: Viṣṇu sleeps for four months from the Āṣāḍha bright ekādaśī AT NIGHT and rises from sleep on the Kārtika bright ekādaśī BY DAY. Kane is candid that what the sleep-legend was meant to symbolise is difficult to say, and offers the plausible naturalistic reading that the rains halted long-distance movement, so mythology supplied a corresponding divine inactivity; he also floats, without endorsing, a northern-latitude origin. Record the legend, not the explanation. WHAT IS DONE: worship of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, a night of hymns, and the taking of vows to be kept through the four months. CĀTURMĀSYA START IS ITSELF DISPUTED: the vrata may be begun on Āṣāḍha śukla ekādaśī, or dvādaśī, or the pūrṇimā, or on the day the sun enters Karka — four options in the sources — and however begun it is completed on Kārtika śukla dvādaśī. During the four months a class of food is given up in each: vegetables in Śrāvaṇa, curds in Bhādrapada, milk in Āśvina, pulses in Kārtika. Marriages are barred for the duration, which is why Prabodhinī reopens the wedding season. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits the full ekādaśī apparatus; see ekadashi-shukla.

name: Prabodhinī (Devotthāna) Ekādaśī
summary: The ekādaśī of Kārtika on which Viṣṇu is held to wake from his four-month sleep, closing Cāturmāsya.
note: Śukla, so no reckoning field. Also Devotthāna, Deva Uttāna, Uttānā Ekādaśī, Hari Prabodhinī, Deothān. The counterpart of Devśayanī: Kane's formulation is that Viṣṇu sleeps from the Āṣāḍha bright ekādaśī at night and rises on the Kārtika bright ekādaśī by day. WHAT IS DONE: waking of the deity, Viṣṇu-pūjā, and the end of the four-month restrictions. Because marriages are barred through Cāturmāsya, this ekādaśī opens the wedding season, and Tulasī Vivāha — the symbolic marriage of Viṣṇu to Lakṣmī in the form of the tulasī plant — is performed on or about it, running into Kārtika Pūrṇimā four days later. A TERMINUS AMBIGUITY WORTH RECORDING: Kane's cāturmāsya chapter says the vrata is completed on Kārtika śukla dvādaśī, the twelfth, not the eleventh; the vrata's END and this ekādaśī are adjacent but not identical, and sources vary on which carries the concluding rite. Do not silently merge them. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits the full ekādaśī apparatus; see ekadashi-shukla. Note that where a Vaiṣṇava aruṇodaya-vedha displaces the fast to dvādaśī, the fast day and the cāturmāsya terminus coincide.

name: Vaikuṇṭha Ekādaśī
summary: The waxing-fortnight ekādaśī falling within the solar month of Dhanus, on which the gate of Vaikuṇṭha is held to open.
note:
MARKED DISPUTED BECAUSE THE ANCHOR IS HYBRID AND MBF HAS NO KIND FOR IT. The observance is defined SOLAR-LUNARLY: it is the śukla-pakṣa ekādaśī that falls while the sun stands in sidereal Dhanus — the Tamil month Mārgaḻi, Dhanurmāsa — which is why it lands between about 16 December and 13 January. In lunar-month terms that ekādaśī is USUALLY Mārgaśīrṣa śukla 11, in which case it coincides with Mokṣadā Ekādaśī, but it can instead be Pauṣa śukla 11, in which case it coincides with Pauṣa Putradā Ekādaśī. Neither lunar month is the answer on its own; the solar constraint decides, and in some years pañcāṅgas following purely lunar naming and those following the Dhanurmāsa definition disagree. I have therefore recorded both lunar possibilities as variants rather than choosing. Śukla tithis are named alike in both amānta and pūrṇimānta reckoning, so no reckoning field. NAMES: Mukkoṭi Ekādaśi in Telugu-speaking regions; Guruvāyūr Ekādaśi in Kerala; the Śaiva observance of the same day as Trikoṭi Ekādaśī. WHAT IS DONE: a full fast with a night vigil and pre-dawn temple visit; the Padmapurāṇa legend of Yogamāyā slaying Murāsura, from whom Viṣṇu names the goddess Ekādaśī, makes this the FIRST ekādaśī and a Dhanurmāsa śukla-pakṣa one. At Srirangam the Paramapada Vāsal is opened on this day alone and the celebration runs twenty days as pagal pattu and irā pattu; at Tirumala the Vaikuṇṭa Dvāram is opened. The Viṣṇupurāṇa claim that fasting here equals fasting on the other twenty-three is māhātmya, and stands against the Vaiṣṇava rule that all twenty-four are obligatory anyway. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits the ekādaśī vedha apparatus; see ekadashi-shukla.

REGIONAL SPLIT, not a disagreement to resolve: the same Ekādaśī is named Mārgaśīrṣa in the southern amānta reckoning and Pauṣa in the northern pūrṇimānta one. Both anchors are given; a consumer should show the one its audience keeps.

name: Adhika Māsa Ekādaśī (Padminī and Paramā)
summary: The two ekādaśīs of the intercalary month, which are observed under their own names even though other vratas are suspended.
note:
THIS ENTRY EXISTS TO RECORD THE EXPLICIT EXCEPTION TO THE NO-VRATA-IN-ADHIKA-MĀSA RULE. The general rule is well attested: Gārgya, quoted by Hemādri, holds that in an intercalary month one should neither begin a vrata nor perform its udyāpana; Kane states that Rāmanavamī is not celebrated in an intercalary Caitra and that the same applies to Janmāṣṭamī and other vratas; and for the ancestral rites he states separately that Mahālayaśrāddha is not to be performed in a malamāsa. Observances wait for the nija month. BUT the ekādaśīs of the adhika month are not suspended — they were given their own names precisely because they are kept. Kane records that for the twenty-four ekādaśīs of the ordinary year and for THE TWO EKĀDAŚĪS OF THE INTERCALARY MONTH separate names were invented, and refers to Padmapurāṇa VI.64–65 for the names of the dark and bright halves. The adhika month is itself dignified as Puruṣottama Māsa. Saṅkaṣṭī Caturthī likewise carries a thirteenth vrata-kathā and a thirteenth name and pīṭha of Gaṇeśa reserved for the adhika month, which is a second, independent attestation that the monthly cycle continues through it. THE NAME-TO-PAKṢA ASSIGNMENT IS DISPUTED, which is why this is one entry and not two. The prevailing usage makes Padminī the śukla-pakṣa ekādaśī and Paramā the kṛṣṇa-pakṣa one; some published tables reverse them; the OCR of Kane's footnote citing Padma VI.64–65 does not resolve which name the Purāṇa attaches to which half. I record both tithis under one key rather than assert an assignment I cannot verify. SUNRISE OWNERSHIP: inherits the ordinary ekādaśī vedha apparatus.

OCCURS ONLY IN AN INTERCALARY MONTH, so in most years it does not occur at all and an empty result is the correct answer. This is the opposite of the usual rule that festivals wait for the nija month — these two belong to the repeat itself.

name: Śāradīya Navarātri
summary: The autumn nine-night festival of the Goddess, the principal Devī observance of the year.
note: Opens with ghaṭasthāpana / kalaśa-sthāpana on Śukla Pratipadā and runs through Navamī; Vijayā Daśamī follows as a separate day. The Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī) is recited, in daily portions or as a single pāṭha. CAVEAT: the festival is always nine TITHIS but not always nine civil days — a kṣaya (omitted) tithi shortens it to eight, a vṛddhi (doubled) tithi stretches it to ten, and pañcāṅgas differ over which civil day carries which tithi. In Bengal, Assam and Odisha the effective festival is the five days Ṣaṣṭhī–Daśamī (Durgā Pūjā), not nine. Per the standard nibandha rule the observance is never held in an adhika Āśvina; it waits for the nija month.

name: Mahālayā Amāvasyā
summary: The new moon closing Pitṛpakṣa and, in Bengal, opening Devīpakṣa — the overture to Durgā Pūjā.

Tarpaṇa is offered to the ancestors at dawn on the riverbank (sarva-pitṛ-amāvasyā); in Bengal the same morning marks the turn from the fortnight of the dead to the fortnight of the Goddess, and image-makers perform cakṣudāna, the painting of Durgā's eyes. RECKONING: named Āśvina Kṛṣṇa Amāvasyā in the purnimanta system used across North India; the identical day is Bhādrapada Amāvasyā in the amanta system used in Bengal, the Deccan and the South. Verified as 10 October 2026. Note that Mahālayā is exactly one lunation before Kālī Pūjā, which the amanta system in turn calls Āśvina Amāvasyā — the two 'Āśvina amāvasyās' in circulation are different new moons, and conflating them is the commonest error in this part of the calendar.

note:
Worshipped at niśītha, the middle watch of the night, when the amāvasyā is at its darkest; the same new moon on which the rest of India worships Lakṣmī. name: Kālī Caudas (Bhūta Caturdaśī)
summary: The dark fourteenth before the Dīvālī new moon, kept for Kālī and for the warding of spirits.
note: In Gujarat and Rajasthan the night is Kālī Caudas, given to Kālī and to rites against malign influence; in Bengal the same night is Bhūta Caturdaśī, when fourteen lamps are lit and fourteen leafy greens eaten for the fourteen forebears; across North India it is Naraka Caturdaśī or Choṭī Dīvālī. RECKONING: named Kārtika Kṛṣṇa Caturdaśī in the purnimanta system; the same day is Āśvina Kṛṣṇa Caturdaśī in the amanta system. It is the day immediately before Kālī Pūjā. Verified as 7 November 2026.

regionalVariants.note: Kālī Caudas; the specifically Śākta reading of the night.
Bhūta Caturdaśī: fourteen lamps, fourteen greens (choddo shaak), for the ancestors and against spirits.
Naraka Caturdaśī / Choṭī Dīvālī, framed around Kṛṣṇa's killing of Narakāsura rather than around Kālī.

name: Ratantī Kālī Pūjā
summary: A winter night-worship of Kālī on the dark fourteenth of the Māgha fortnight.
note:
One of the four great Kālī nights of the Bengali year. Kept especially at Kālīghāṭ and Tārāpīṭh. RECKONING: sources give the day as Māgha Kṛṣṇa Caturdaśī, which is purnimanta naming — it is the caturdaśī immediately preceding Maunī Amāvasyā. In the amanta system used by Bengali lunar-month naming the identical day is Pauṣa Kṛṣṇa Caturdaśī; Bengali usage reaches the name 'Māgha' by way of the solar month Māgh in which it falls, not the lunar one. In 2026 Maunī Amāvasyā is 18 January, placing Ratantī on 17 January. Worship is at niśītha, as at Kālī Pūjā.

Day rule: niśītha — a niśītha Kālī observance.

sources.note: States 'Ratanti Kali Puja — observed on Magha Krishna Chaturdashi'.
Used to identify which caturdaśī is meant and to establish that the naming is purnimanta.

name: Phalahāriṇī Kālī Pūjā
summary: The Jyeṣṭha new-moon worship of Kālī as 'she who takes away the fruits of action'.
note:
Kālī is invoked here as Phalahāriṇī, the remover of the fruits of karma. The night carries particular weight in the Ramakrishna tradition: on this amāvasyā in 1872 Ramakrishna worshipped Sarada Devi as Ṣoḍaśī at Dakshineswar, and the anniversary is kept as Ṣoḍaśī Pūjā across the Ramakrishna Math and Mission. RECKONING: this is Jyeṣṭha Kṛṣṇa Amāvasyā in the amanta system, which is what Bengali usage means; the same day is Āṣāḍha Kṛṣṇa Amāvasyā in the purnimanta system. It is NOT the amāvasyā that North India calls Jyeṣṭha Amāvasyā (Vaṭ Sāvitrī), which is one lunation earlier. ADHIKA MONTH: 2026 has an adhika Jyeṣṭha; the observance belongs to the nija month, so it falls at the close of nija Jyeṣṭha in mid-July 2026, not in the intercalary month of May–June.

Day rule: niśītha — a niśītha Kālī observance.

name: Kauśikī Amāvasyā
summary: The monsoon new moon held to be the most potent night of the year for Tārā, above all at Tārāpīṭh.
note: The principal Tārā occasion of the Bengali Śākta year. Tārāpīṭh keeps it as the night on which Bāmākhepā attained siddhi, and it draws the largest pilgrimage of the site's calendar. RECKONING: Śrāvaṇa Kṛṣṇa Amāvasyā in the amanta system used by the Bengali calendar; the same day is Bhādrapada Kṛṣṇa Amāvasyā in the purnimanta system. It falls in the Bengali solar month Bhādra, one lunation BEFORE Mahālayā — the two are frequently conflated and are not the same new moon. For 2026 the Bengali calendar's Śrāvaṇa kṛṣṇa paksha runs through early September, placing this amāvasyā around 11 September, with Mahālayā a month later on 10 October. CLOSED MATERIAL: the Tārā sādhanā associated with the night is dīkṣā-bound and is not recorded here.

name: Lalitā Jayantī (Tripurasundarī / Ṣoḍaśī)
summary: The Māgha full moon kept as the appearance day of Lalitā Tripurasundarī, third of the Mahāvidyās.
note: The observance of the day is public: recitation of the Lalitā Sahasranāma and Lalitā Triśatī, and Śrīcakra pūjā where a qualified practitioner is present. Because Pūrṇimā is the hinge on which the two month systems meet, amanta and purnimanta agree on the name Māgha Pūrṇimā and no reckoning field is needed. CLOSED MATERIAL: Śrīvidyā proper — the pañcadaśī and ṣoḍaśī vidyās, the Śrīcakra navāvaraṇa sequence and the associated dhyāna — is transmitted only by dīkṣā and is deliberately not recorded here. CAVEAT: some almanacs additionally list a separate 'Tripurasundarī Jayantī' or 'Ṣoḍaśī Jayantī'; whether these are distinct occasions or alternative names for this same day could not be established, so only the Māgha Pūrṇimā occasion is entered.

name: Dhūmāvatī Jayantī
summary: The appearance day of Dhūmāvatī, the widow-goddess and seventh Mahāvidyā, on Jyeṣṭha Śukla Aṣṭamī.
note: The public observance is centred on the Dhūmāvatī temple at Varanasi, which is one of very few temples anywhere where she is the principal deity. Śākta sources are explicit that hers is not a householder cult: married people are advised against her worship, which is held to suit renunciants, lone wanderers and widows. CAVEAT: her ordinary (non-jayantī) worship day is given in the same sources as a kṛṣṇa-pakṣa caturdaśī, so 'the day of Dhūmāvatī' means different things depending on whether the jayantī or the recurring rite is meant; do not merge them. ADHIKA MONTH: 2026 has an adhika Jyeṣṭha, so the jayantī belongs to nija Jyeṣṭha (late June 2026), not to the intercalary month. CLOSED MATERIAL: her sādhanā is initiatory; occasion and date only are recorded.

sources.note: Quoted: 'It falls on the "ashtami" (8th day) during the "Shukla Paksha" ... in the "Jyestha" month of the Hindu calendar.' General-interest almanac source; the only one located that states the tithi explicitly.

name: Mātaṅgī Jayantī
summary: The appearance day of Mātaṅgī, ninth of the Mahāvidyās, on Vaiśākha Śukla Tṛtīyā.
note: Falls on the same tithi as Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, verified independently as Vaiśākha Śukla Tṛtīyā (19 April 2026). Mātaṅgī is the outlier of the Mahāvidyā set in the matter of access: the sources state that no purificatory fast or preparatory rite is prescribed for her worship and that anyone may approach her, including those held unfit or uninitiated for other deities — so unlike most of the ten, her cult is not gated by dīkṣā. She is identified with Śyāmalā/Rājamātaṅgī in the Śrīvidyā tradition, where the material does become initiatory; that layer is not recorded here. CAVEAT: the tithi is attested only through general-interest reporting, not through a critical or Purāṇic source.

name: Bagalāmukhī Jayantī
summary: The appearance day of Bagalāmukhī, eighth of the Mahāvidyās, the stambhana goddess.
note: DISPUTED — DATE NOT VERIFIED. Hindi pañcāṅgas and the major Bagalāmukhī temples (Datia and Nalkheda in Madhya Pradesh, Bankhandi in Himachal Pradesh) are widely reported to keep the jayantī on Vaiśākha Śukla Aṣṭamī, and that is the anchor recorded here, but no pañcāṅga or scholarly source could be reached in this pass that states it directly: the encyclopaedic article on the goddess gives no jayantī date at all, and the almanac sites consulted have no page for it. Treat the anchor as the commonly published claim rather than as verified. If the anchor is wrong, the likeliest correction is a different tithi within Vaiśākha śukla pakṣa. CLOSED MATERIAL: Bagalāmukhī's practice is strongly initiatory and is associated with abhicāra applications; only the occasion is recorded, with no mantra, prayoga or dhyāna.

sources.note: Consulted and found to give NO jayantī date; names the Bankhandi, Datia and Nalkheda temples and the Tantrasāra and Rudrayāmala as textual sources. Recorded here as negative evidence.

name: Chinnamastā Jayantī
summary: The appearance day of Chinnamastā, fifth of the Mahāvidyās, the self-decapitated goddess.
note: DISPUTED — DATE NOT VERIFIED. The commonly published date is Vaiśākha Śukla Caturdaśī, the same tithi as Narasiṃha Jayantī (independently verified as 29 April 2026), and that is the anchor recorded here; but no pañcāṅga or scholarly source reached in this pass states it, and the encyclopaedic article on the goddess gives no jayantī date. Treat as the common claim, not as established. CLOSED MATERIAL: her worship is explicitly restricted in the sources — individual worship is 'mainly restricted to heroic Tāntrikas', temples to her alone are rare, and the Tantrasāra directs a householder to invoke her only in abstract terms. Nothing beyond the occasion and its putative date is recorded.

name: Jagaddhātrī Pūjā
summary: The Kārtika worship of Durgā as Jagaddhātrī, Upholder of the World, a distinctively Bengali festival.
note: Held on Kārtika Śukla Navamī. Practice divides on duration: many places keep only the Navamī tithi, while Krishnanagar and Chandannagar run a five-day form from Ṣaṣṭhī, so the entry carries no lasts field and the variation is noted instead. The Krishnanagar tradition is traced to Mahārāja Kṛṣṇacandra, whose imprisonment by Alivardi Khan and release on Vijayā Daśamī is said to have prompted a compensating autumn festival; the Chasa Para 'Burima' image has been kept since 1772. The earliest textual notice of the goddess is in the Kālaviveka of the smārta Śūlapāṇi (c. 1375–1460), which makes this the best-documented of the Bengali Śākta festivals in pre-modern sources. Śukla-pakṣa tithi, so no reckoning field is required. Verified as 18 November 2026.

name: Ambubācī Melā
summary: The annual menstruation of the goddess Kāmākhyā, when the temple closes and the great Tantric pilgrimage gathers.
note: The Kāmākhyā temple on Nīlācala closes for three days while the goddess is held to be in her courses; the Brahmaputra beside it is said to run red. On the fourth day the image is bathed and the doors reopen — Ambubācī Nivṛtti — and prasāda is distributed. It is the largest gathering of Tantric practitioners in eastern India. ANCHOR IS RECONSTRUCTED: the source consulted states only that the mela falls in the Assamese month Āhāra 'when the sun transits to the zodiac of Mithuna'. Assamese and Bengali pañjikās fix it more precisely at the seventh day of Āhāra, that is, the Sun's ingress into the Ārdrā nakṣatra, which is nirayaṇa (sidereal) solar longitude 66°40′ — seven days after Mithuna Saṅkrānti at 60°. The degrees value below is that ingress. The civil date therefore shifts with the ayanāṃśa a given pañjikā uses. Sources also differ on whether the observance is three days (the closure) or four (closure plus Nivṛtti); three is recorded, per the source consulted.

sources.note: Quoted: celebrated 'during the Assamese month Ahar, around the middle of June when the sun transits to the zodiac of Mithuna'; 'The temple remains closed for three days'; after three days the goddess is bathed and 'the doors of the temple are reopened and prasad is distributed'.

name: Basantī Pūjā
summary: The spring Durgā Pūjā of Bengal, held in Caitra — the canonical season the autumn festival departs from.
note: Runs Ṣaṣṭhī to Daśamī inside Caitra Śukla Pakṣa, mirroring the autumn festival's five days, and is much the smaller observance in modern Bengal despite being the older-seasoned one. Its importance is structural: the autumn Durgā Pūjā is called akāl bodhon, 'untimely awakening', precisely because Basantī is the timely one, and the Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa's story of Rāma waking the Goddess out of season presupposes it. Runs concurrently with Vāsantika (Caitra) Navarātri, which is entered separately. Śukla-pakṣa tithis, so no reckoning field is needed. CAVEAT: the five-day span is recorded from the parallel with the autumn festival and from Bengali usage; the almanac summaries consulted did not list Basantī Pūjā as a separate entry, so the day boundaries are less firmly sourced than those of Śāradīya Durgā Pūjā.

sources.note: The akāl bodhon narrative, which presupposes spring as the proper season for waking the Goddess.

name: Sarasvatī Pūjā (Vasanta Pañcamī)
summary: The Māgha bright fifth, kept in Bengal as the year's principal domestic Devī festival after Durgā and Kālī.
note: In Bengal, Assam and Odisha the day is a full pratimā pūjā to Sarasvatī in homes, schools and pandals, with hāte-khaḍi — a child's first letters written under the goddess's eye. Elsewhere in North India it is Vasanta Pañcamī, the opening of spring, with yellow dress and offerings. Verified as 23 January 2026, Māgha Śukla Pañcamī. Included here as part of the Devī-centred calendar although Sarasvatī sits outside the Mahāvidyā set; in Śākta reckoning she is one of the three functional aspects distributed across Navarātri.

regionalVariants.note: Kept as Sarasvatī Pūjā with clay images and hāte-khaḍi; effectively a public festival.

name: Kojāgarī Lakṣmī Pūjā
summary: The Āśvina full moon, kept in Bengal as an all-night vigil to Lakṣmī four days after Vijayā Daśamī.
note: The name is from ko jāgarti — 'who is awake?' — the question the goddess is said to ask as she moves over the world at night, rewarding the wakeful. Observed with a night-long vigil, alpanā at the threshold, and offerings of ciṛe and nārikel. It is the Bengali Lakṣmī festival, standing where the Dīvālī Lakṣmī Pūjā stands elsewhere; in the Mahāvidyā scheme Lakṣmī corresponds to Kamalā, the tenth Vidyā, though the Kojāgarī rite itself is not Tantric. Pūrṇimā, so both month systems agree and no reckoning field is needed. Verified as 25 October 2026, Āśvina Śukla Pūrṇimā (also Śarad Pūrṇimā).

regionalVariants.note: The principal Lakṣmī observance of the year, displacing the Dīvālī Lakṣmī Pūjā, which Bengal gives to Kālī instead.
Kept as Śarad Pūrṇimā with kheer left under the moon; the Lakṣmī vigil is comparatively minor here.
